stories.headline: Broncos Open Training Camp in New $175 Million Dove Valley Practice Facility
stories.summary:
The Denver Broncos officially began their 2026 training camp Tuesday at their newly completed $175 million practice facility in Englewood, marking a significant upgrade for the franchise under the Walton-Penner ownership group. The building features a redesigned locker room, centralized weight room, underground parking, and a lobby showcasing the team's three Lombardi Trophies behind glass paneling with mass timber beams and Broncos branding throughout.

All-Pro cornerback Pat Surtain II called the facility "state-of-the-art" and said it exceeded his expectations, adding that it may be unlike anything else in the NFL. Offensive lineman Quinn Meinerz was among the veterans who toured the new headquarters Monday, praising the elimination of cross-lot treks to separate practice buildings.

The facility's completion comes after construction was briefly halted in June following the death of 31-year-old worker Sven Eryk Johnson. An OSHA investigation into Johnson's death remains ongoing.

The new locker room in particular addresses a long-standing weakness: the Broncos received an "F" grade from the NFL Players' Association on locker room quality in 2025. The facility is seen as a statement of intent by ownership as the franchise pursues its first Super Bowl appearance in more than a decade.

stories.headline: Nuggets Hire Dave Joerger as Lead Assistant, Raising Questions About Coach Adelman's Standing
stories.summary:
The Denver Nuggets have agreed to bring on Dave Joerger as lead assistant coach under head coach David Adelman, according to ESPN's Shams Charania. The 52-year-old Joerger brings extensive NBA head coaching experience, having compiled a 147-99 record with three playoff berths in Memphis from 2013 to 2016 before a less successful stint in Sacramento and assistant roles with Philadelphia and Milwaukee under Doc Rivers.

The hire is widely interpreted as a move by the organization to add veteran oversight to Adelman's staff after a disappointing playoff exit, in which the Nuggets were eliminated by a Minnesota team missing Anthony Edwards. The front office previously offered Adelman a public vote of confidence from Josh Kroenke following that series.

Joerger is regarded in league circles as a defensive specialist, though his teams' defensive ratings have shown inconsistency over his career. The Nuggets have ranked in the bottom ten in defensive rating in each of the past two regular seasons, finishing 21st in 2024-25 and 2025-26.

Columnist Mark Kiszla and others have noted that the arrangement — sometimes compared to a "coach-in-waiting" structure — could complicate Adelman's authority even as the team publicly frames it as a complementary hire.

stories.headline: Poll Shows Colorado Springs' 5th Congressional District Competitive for First Time, Democrat Within 1 Point of Incumbent
stories.summary:
A new poll conducted for Democrat Jessica Killin's campaign shows her trailing Republican U.S. Rep. Jeff Crank by just one percentage point in Colorado's 5th Congressional District, the Colorado Springs-centered seat that has never sent a Democrat to Congress. The survey, conducted July 16-21 among 450 likely voters by Global Strategy Group, showed Crank at 45% and Killin at 44%, with 11% undecided and a margin of error of 4.6 percentage points.

Killin, an Army veteran and former chief of staff to Doug Emhoff, raised $3.1 million through the end of June — more than Crank's $1.8 million for the same period. The House Majority PAC, tied to House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, has already reserved television advertising time in the Colorado Springs/Pueblo market ahead of November.

The poll attributes Killin's competitiveness to voter familiarity with her candidacy and broad disapproval of President Trump among unaffiliated voters in the district. Demographic shifts in the Colorado Springs area, long a Republican stronghold, are also cited as a factor.

National Democrats have signaled they are prepared to invest in the race if they determine it is winnable. The Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee is expected to finalize its level of engagement as the national House map develops in the coming months.

stories.headline: History Colorado Board Condemns Federal Proposal to Weaken National Historic Preservation Act
stories.summary:
History Colorado's board of directors has formally condemned a proposed federal rule that would alter Section 106 of the National Historic Preservation Act, calling it a threat to collaboration and to protections for archaeological, cultural, and historic sites. The draft rule, advanced July 24 by the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation — an independent federal agency with Trump-appointed members — would consolidate federal decision-making authority, limit consultation with state, tribal, and local governments, and narrow the definition of what qualifies as "historic."

History Colorado president and CEO Dawn DiPrince said the proposed revisions would "erode our shared commitment to preserve our shared culture and heritage" and that collaboration is the central tenet of the existing Act. She noted the statement was notable given that public opposition to federal actions is rare among state historical societies, which rely on federal grants and are officially nonpartisan.

History Colorado receives just over $1.2 million annually in federal funding to support the State Historic Preservation Office and operates the History Colorado Center in Denver along with nearly a dozen other museums and historic sites statewide. Its total 2024-25 budget was approximately $40.8 million.

DiPrince declined to address whether the public statement could put that federal funding at risk. The board is appointed by Gov. Jared Polis to three-year terms.

stories.headline: EchoStar Closes $23 Billion Spectrum Sale to AT&T, Retires Significant Debt
stories.summary:
Englewood-based EchoStar has finalized its $23 billion spectrum sale to AT&T, using the proceeds to retire billions of dollars in debt and fund a trust required by the Federal Communications Commission following the company's failed attempt to build out a nationwide 5G network. The deal represents one of the largest spectrum transactions in U.S. telecommunications history.

EchoStar, the satellite and wireless company controlled by the Ergen family, had accumulated substantial debt in part through its costly and ultimately unsuccessful 5G buildout efforts. The FCC-mandated trust is tied to obligations the company took on during the spectrum acquisition process.

The transaction marks a significant restructuring milestone for EchoStar, which is headquartered in the Denver metro area and has been a major player in the region's technology and telecommunications sector. The company's future operations following the sale are expected to focus on its remaining satellite and broadband businesses.

stories.headline: Severe Thunderstorm and Flood Watches Continue Through Tuesday Evening; More Storms Expected Wednesday
stories.summary:
A severe thunderstorm watch remained in effect across the Denver metro and eastern Plains through 8 p.m. Tuesday, with flood watches active on the eastern Plains until 10 p.m. and a flash flood watch running until midnight for the Aspen Acres burn scar to the south. The storms have produced flooding and severe weather from the mountains to the plains throughout the day.

Wednesday is forecast to bring a similar pattern, with thunderstorms developing in the mountains around midday and pushing into the I-25 corridor and Denver metro between 1 and 3 p.m. Those storms are expected to be capable of heavy rainfall, localized flooding, gusty winds, and small hail, with high temperatures reaching the lower 90s.

Storm chances are expected to diminish Thursday through Friday as the monsoon pattern weakens. Temperatures will climb through the weekend, with highs near 100 degrees possible by Sunday — approaching but likely short of the all-time record of 103 degrees set on that date in 2008.

Another round of rain chances is forecast to return by the middle of next week, with temperatures dropping back to the lower 90s by next Tuesday.

stories.headline: Missing Woman's Body Recovered from Lake Pueblo State Park
stories.summary:
Colorado Parks and Wildlife officers recovered the body of a missing woman from Lake Pueblo State Park on Monday afternoon after a search that lasted several hours. The woman, whose identity has not been publicly released, was reported missing by her family after she was last seen Sunday evening, and authorities were notified around noon Monday.

Wildlife officers found her fishing pole and personal belongings on the north side of the park near Yucca Flats Campground, along a cliff overlooking the water. The search was complicated by steep cliffs and large boulders in the area before her body was located shortly after 5 p.m.

The Pueblo County Coroner's Office will release the woman's identity and cause of death. Lake Pueblo State Park manager Joe Stadterman expressed condolences to the victim's family and praised the professionalism of officers and partner agencies involved in the recovery operation.

stories.headline: Colorado Ranked No. 1 in Education by U.S. News and World Report
stories.summary:
Governor Jared Polis and state education leaders celebrated Colorado receiving the top ranking in education from U.S. News and World Report, citing investments in K-12 funding, early childhood education, and higher education affordability as driving factors. The ranking acknowledges progress on a range of metrics from preschool enrollment to college-level coursework participation rates.

State legislative leaders including House Speaker Julie McCluskie, Senate President James Coleman, and Joint Budget Committee Chair Rep. Emily Sirota credited the state's investments in universal preschool, free school meals, and K-12 funding reforms for the recognition. University of Colorado President Todd Saliman said the ranking reflects strong returns on investment from the state's colleges and universities.

Despite the recognition, state officials cautioned that more work remains to fully fund K-12 schools. Several legislators noted that teachers have persevered through difficult budget years and that adequate public school funding remains an ongoing priority.

The announcement comes at a notable moment for Colorado education policy, which has also recently seen debates over cellphone restrictions in schools and reduced mental health funding heading into the new academic year.

stories.headline: Aspen Trees Can Slow or Stop Wildfires, Study Finds; Colorado Foresters Confirm the Approach
stories.summary:
A new study from McGill University confirms that stands of aspen trees can act as effective barriers to wildfire spread, slowing or stopping flames even under conditions conducive to high-severity fires. Researchers analyzed nearly 80% of Canada's aspen across four ecozones using improved remote sensor networks, finding that aspen burned at lower severity than surrounding tree species and held up as a firebreak even on hot, dry days.

Colorado State Forest Service associate director Aaron Green said the findings align with what state foresters have long understood in practice. "It's something that we've known all along," Green said, adding that diversity in forest stand structure is recognized as a key tool for limiting the spread of disturbances like wildfire.

The research supports ongoing Colorado efforts to diversify forests heavily damaged by pine beetle infestations, drought, and previous wildfires. State forester Matt McCombs has also emphasized the importance of species diversity at higher elevations to protect diminishing snowpack from accelerated melting.

The findings carry particular relevance for Colorado this summer, as the state's wildfire season has already surpassed 242,000 acres burned. Aspen are noted as the first species to reestablish in moist areas after a fire, eventually giving way to longer-lived conifers.

stories.headline: Denver Post Names 150 Most Notable Coloradans in Colorado Sesquicentennial Celebration
stories.summary:
The Denver Post has published its list of the 150 most influential or notable Coloradans as part of coverage marking Colorado's 150th anniversary of statehood. The list was compiled through a combination of reader nominations — with Titanic survivor Molly Brown topping reader suggestions — and input from community members, with the Post applying criteria around depth of Colorado roots and demonstrated impact on the state's culture and history.

The list spans a wide range of fields and includes figures of national and international significance, from former Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, whose father founded a graduate school at the University of Denver, to entrepreneur Philip Anschutz, who has donated more than $100 million to the University of Colorado School of Medicine. Musicians, physicians, politicians, and civic leaders are among those recognized.

The Post noted that it excluded notorious figures and weighed known character flaws against historical significance when making inclusion decisions. Some entries pair two individuals whose achievements were considered inseparable.

The list is part of broader Colorado 150 anniversary coverage appearing across Denver-area media and state institutions this year.

stories.headline: Sen. Hickenlooper's Patients Deserve Price Tags Act Advances Out of Committee with Bipartisan Support
stories.summary:
U.S. Senator John Hickenlooper's Patients Deserve Price Tags Act passed out of committee last week with bipartisan support, advancing legislation aimed at improving price transparency in health care. The bill would require providers to give patients clearer upfront cost information before they receive medical services.

The legislation comes as Colorado health care costs and access remain prominent issues, particularly following recent federal Medicaid policy changes that are projected to significantly affect safety-net providers like Denver Health. Hickenlooper has made health care affordability a central focus of his Senate work.

Bipartisan committee support for the measure increases its chances of advancing to a full Senate vote, though the broader legislative calendar and political dynamics in Congress will determine its ultimate fate.

stories.headline: Southeastern Colorado Fishing Economy Threatened as Reservoir Access Closes Over Contract Dispute
stories.summary:
Access to a southeastern Colorado reservoir has been closed due to an unresolved contract dispute, threatening the local fishing economy that depends on the water body for recreational use and tourism revenue. The closure has drawn concern from anglers, outfitters, and local businesses that rely on the reservoir as a destination during the summer season.

Details of the contract dispute and the parties involved were not fully disclosed, but the closure affects public access to a resource that supports jobs and economic activity in a region with limited alternative attractions. Local stakeholders are pressing for a resolution before the peak summer season passes.

The situation adds to a series of water-related challenges facing Colorado this summer, including deepening drought conditions, reduced reservoir levels across the metro area, and flash flood risks tied to the ongoing monsoon pattern.

topStory.headline: Georgia Teen Sentenced to Life Without Parole for Apalachee High School Shooting That Killed Four
topStory.summary:
Barrow County Superior Court Judge Nicholas Primm on Tuesday sentenced 16-year-old Colt Gray to life in prison without the possibility of parole for the Sept. 4, 2024, shooting at Apalachee High School in Winder, Georgia, about 45 miles northeast of Atlanta. Gray had pleaded guilty Friday to 55 counts, including murder, in the attack that killed two teachers and two students.

The four victims were math teacher and football coach Richard "Ricky" Aspinwall, 39; teacher Cristina Irimie, 53; and students Mason Schermerhorn and Christian Angulo, both 14. One additional teacher and eight students were wounded, seven of them by gunfire. Shayna Aspinwall, widow of Richard Aspinwall, told the court the shooting had left survivors with "a life sentence of grief and trauma."

In handing down the sentence, Judge Primm rejected defense arguments that Gray retained the capacity for rehabilitation. "You do not seem to be tormented by what you did. You seem to relish following in the footsteps of the murderers you idolize. You aren't wracked with guilt. You're proud of yourself," Primm said. District Attorney Brad Smith argued there was "no evidence" Gray could develop a conscience, while defense attorney W. Charlton Allen contended his client was "not irretrievably broken" and that parole eligibility would provide "an opportunity of hope."

Investigators testified during the three-day sentencing hearing that Gray had idolized mass shooters and discussed gaining notoriety through a school attack in online conversations with members of what authorities described as a "true crime community." Prosecutors also played recorded phone calls Gray made to his mother, Marcee Gray, from a youth detention facility in the months following the shooting, during which he directed her to search for public commentary about him online and expressed excitement over "fan art" and attention he was receiving.

Because murder carries a mandatory life sentence under Georgia law, the sole question before Judge Primm was whether Gray would ever be eligible for parole; the judge ruled he would not. Smith told reporters after the sentencing that while it was not "a happy day," it was "a relief day," adding that he hoped his office had done honor to the victims and their families. Gray's father, Colin Gray, was previously convicted on charges of second-degree murder and involuntary manslaughter in connection with the shooting.
